name: Unit Bias
description: People often treat one whole unit of something as the natural or appropriate amount, even when the unit size is arbitrary. Finishing one portion, one scoop, or one packaged chunk can feel right regardless of its actual size.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to portion selectors, bundles, checklists, loyalty cards, and packaged tasks: arbitrary unit boundaries can quietly steer how much people take, consume, or feel compelled to complete.
myth_risk_note: The phenomenon is well-evidenced specifically in portion-size and consumption contexts, with a Cochrane meta-analysis confirming a consistent small-to-moderate effect. Broader applications to task completion and non-consumption decision-making are labeled with the same term but lack equivalent direct empirical support, consistent with the entry's existing partial status.
prevalence_note: Known in nutrition, habit, and behavior-design conversations and occasionally useful in product work, but not a mainstream named UX law in ordinary interface critique.

findings.description: A Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 72 studies (food, alcohol, and tobacco domains) found a small-to-moderate effect of portion/package/tableware size on selection and consumption (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.29-0.46), explicitly identifying unit bias -- the perception that one presented unit is the appropriate amount to consume -- as one of the underlying mechanisms, independently confirming Geier, Rozin & Doros' (2006) core single-study finding at meta-analytic scale and across a much broader range of products/contexts.
findings.source_title: Portion, package or tableware size for changing selection and consumption of food, alcohol and tobacco

findings.description: Manipulating unit size changed how much participants took and consumed even when they were free to take as many units as they wanted: larger candy units or scoops produced substantially greater intake, supporting the idea that one perceived "unit" feels like the appropriate amount.
